title: Small Stock Carcasses and Offal Inspection Process

lessons.title: Inspecting at small stock line speed
lessons.html:
The challenge of small stock lines

Sheep and goat lines run much faster than beef lines. Hundreds of carcasses can pass in an hour, especially at big abattoirs in the Karoo, Free State and Northern Cape. In this work experience module you learn to inspect at a working speed while still doing every required step, under the supervision of a qualified inspector.

Offal inspection

Small stock offal is often hung on a hook or placed on a tray matching the carcass. Work in a fixed order:

  1. Lungs: view and palpate for pneumonia, lungworm nodules, abscesses and hydatid cysts.
  2. Heart: view and incise for sheep measles.
  3. Liver: view and palpate for fluke, bladder worms, hydatid cysts and abscesses.
  4. Spleen and green offal: view for abnormalities.

Carcass inspection

  1. View the outside for bruises, grass seeds, dirt and wool.
  2. Palpate the prescapular and prefemoral lymph nodes for caseous lymphadenitis.
  3. View the inside: pleura, peritoneum, diaphragm and kidneys.
  4. Look at colour and smell for jaundice, fever and poor bleeding.

Keeping up safely

  • Position yourself so you can see and reach the whole carcass without twisting.
  • Keep your knife in the steriliser when not cutting.
  • Use both hands well: one palpates, the other holds the knife safely.
  • If too many carcasses pass uninspected, the line must be slowed or stopped. Tell your supervisor; never let carcasses pass uninspected.

Speed comes from practice and a fixed routine, not from skipping steps. Your mentor will watch you inspect a batch and check that every step is done.

lessons.title: Typical findings on a sheep and goat line
lessons.html:
What you will find most often

FindingNotesUsual action
Caseous lymphadenitisAbscesses in lymph nodes, common in older sheep and goatsRemove affected node and area; detain if many
Bladder wormThin cysts on liver and omentumRemove affected parts
Hydatid cystsLiver and lungsCondemn affected organs
Sheep measlesSmall cysts in heart and muscleDetain for veterinarian
Liver flukeThickened bile ductsCondemn liver
PneumoniaFirm, dark red areas in lungsCondemn lungs; check carcass
Grass seedsSeeds in skin and muscle, often in winter-grazed sheepTrim affected areas
BruisingOften from lifting by wool or rough loadingTrim

Goats

Goats are inspected in the same way. Goat carcasses have less fat cover, so bruises and abscesses can be easier to see. Abscesses from caseous lymphadenitis are often found in the head and neck region.

When to detain

Detain any carcass with signs of generalised disease: many abscesses, jaundice, poor bleeding, fever signs, emaciation or measles cysts. Move it with its offal to the detention rail and report to the veterinarian.

Hygiene

Abscesses are full of bacteria. If one bursts, stop, trim the area generously, sterilise the knife and wash your hands. Keep wool and dung away from the meat; small stock carcasses are easily contaminated during skinning, so report repeated contamination to the supervisor so the dressing process can be corrected.

lessons.title: Recording and feedback for small stock
lessons.html:
Records on a fast line

Because so many animals pass, many abattoirs use tally sheets or electronic counters at each station. Each time a part is condemned, mark it against the right lot or producer. At the end of each lot, totals are written up.

What the records show

  • High numbers of bladder worm, hydatid and measles findings in a lot show that farm dogs are carrying tapeworms. The farmer should deworm dogs regularly and stop feeding them raw offal or letting them eat carcasses in the veld.
  • Many fluke livers point to wet grazing and the need for a fluke control plan with the farmer's vet.
  • Lots with many caseous lymphadenitis abscesses may point to shearing wounds and poor hygiene during shearing and dipping.
  • Heavy bruising points to handling and transport problems.

This feedback helps farmers lose less income from condemnations, and helps state veterinary services track diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Your logbook

Record daily: number of carcasses inspected, which station you worked, conditions found and detentions. Ask your mentor to sign when you can work each station independently and at line speed. Note any difficult cases and what you learned from the veterinarian's final judgement.

Key points

  • Small stock lines are fast; build speed through a fixed routine, never by skipping steps.
  • Palpate the prescapular and prefemoral lymph nodes on every carcass.
  • Detain carcasses with generalised signs or measles cysts.
  • Record findings per lot or producer using tally sheets or counters.
  • Feedback on tapeworm cysts helps farmers deworm dogs and stop feeding raw offal.
